1352.title: The guest at the hermitage
1352.hook: Shakuntala misses a guest at the gate and a curse follows: why Hindu homes treat the guest as God
1352.carry: the guest is treated as god
1352.howItsDone: Many Hindu families still greet a guest with water, a seat and food before anything else; Kalidasa's play about Shakuntala is still read, staged and danced in India and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child is your own self, born again: Shakuntala in the king's hall, holding her son's hand and telling a king who claimed not to know her the truth about himself.
screen: `A CHILD IS YOUR OWN SELF, BORN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: A sage stands at the gate of a forest hermitage and calls out. Inside, a young woman sits lost in thoughts of her husband, and doesn't hear him. That missed welcome sets off a curse, a lost ring, and a king who forgets his wife. It's Shakuntala again, but not as the Mahabharata tells it. This is the poet Kalidasa's play, and its whole plot turns on a guest.
screen: `A SAGE AT THE GATE.` → `NO ONE GREETS HIM.` → `A WHOLE PLOT TURNS ON A GUEST.`

segments.voice: In the epic, Shakuntala tells the king the truth, a voice from the sky backs her, and the king says, in paraphrase, that he knew her all along, but wanted his people to hear it from heaven so no one would doubt the child. There, the forgetting is a choice. In Kalidasa's play, the sage Durvasa, famous for his temper, arrives at the hermitage. Shakuntala, dreaming of the king, doesn't greet him. So he curses her: the one you're thinking of will forget you. A friend begs for mercy, and the curse is softened: a token will bring the memory back. The token is the ring, and the ring slips into a sacred pool. Why would a missed greeting matter so much? Kalidasa's audience would have known why. An old Upanishad, the Taittiriya, gives a student a parting list: treat your mother as a god, your father as a god, your teacher as a god, and the guest as a god. Atithi devo bhava. A guest at the door is met with water, a seat and food. Shakuntala's fault isn't cruelty. It's love so wrapped up in itself that it misses the person standing at the gate, and many readers take that as the play's quiet lesson. In the end, a fisherman finds the ring inside a fish, the king remembers, and at last he finds their son prying open a lion cub's mouth to count its teeth. In the epic the boy is named Bharata, and the royal line takes its name from him. Tradition hears his name in Bharat, one of India's own names for itself, though other stories lay claim to that name too.
screen: `IN THE EPIC, THE KING CHOOSES TO FORGET` · `IN THE PLAY, A GUEST NO ONE GREETED` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST AS GOD` · `THE RING, THE FISH, THE BOY BHARATA`

segments.voice: Think of the next person likely to come to your door. In many Hindu homes a guest is offered water before anything else is said. Picture yourself looking up and handing them that glass, as if God were at the door. If you pray, ask to see God in whoever comes today. If you don't, simply hold the wish to really see them.

1353.title: The offering and the jackal
1353.hook: Andal calls herself an offering already set before the Lord; why food for God is offered before anyone tastes it
1353.carry: what's offered to god is set apart
1353.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava Hindus honor Andal as one of the Alvars and recite her Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli in temples and homes; in many Hindu homes, food is offered to God before anyone eats, and comes back as prasad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guest is treated as god, and Shakuntala's story told twice: a king who chooses to forget, and a king cursed to forget until a ring comes back in a fish. Today, a poet who speaks for herself.

An offering is laid out for the gods. Priests have prepared it with care, by the rules, for the sacred fire. Then a jackal slips in from the forest and sniffs at it. Ruined. Nobody could offer it now. That rough little picture comes from a young woman's poem, and she's using it about herself: what would happen to her if anyone so much as talked of marrying her to a man. The woman is Andal, and today she speaks for herself.
screen: `AN OFFERING FOR THE GODS.` → `A JACKAL FROM THE FOREST.` → `ANDAL SPEAKS FOR HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Year three met Andal in the Tiruppavai, one cowherd girl among many. Her other work, the Nachiyar Tirumoli, the sacred words of the lady, is her own voice. Take the jackal verse, in paraphrase. My heart is set on the Lord who holds the conch and the wheel. If anyone speaks of giving me to a mortal man, I won't live. It would be like the offering made for the gods being sniffed by a jackal of the forest. She doesn't say marriage is bad. She borrows a picture every Hindu kitchen knows. Food made for God is set apart. In many homes no one tastes it first; it's placed before the Lord, and only then does it come back to the family as prasad, a blessed gift. Andal says she is that food, already offered. Now notice whom she asks for help. The same book opens with her pleading with Kama, the god of desire, sweeping the ground and drawing in the sand for him, asking him to join her to the Lord. Sri Vaishnava teachers have a word for giving yourself wholly to God: sharanagati, taking refuge, surrender. Many of them read Andal's longing as the soul's own, belonging to the Lord before it belongs to anyone. Other readers also hear a young woman saying whom she will and won't belong to. The tradition never had to pick one. It counts her among the Alvars, the poet-saints, and keeps singing her verses.
screen: `THE OFFERING AND THE JACKAL` · `FOOD FOR GOD IS SET APART` · `PRASAD: IT COMES BACK AS A GIFT` · `SHARANAGATI: TAKING REFUGE`

segments.voice: Before your next meal or drink today, pause with it in front of you. Many Hindus offer their food to God first, silently or with a short prayer, before the first bite, so the meal comes back to them as prasad. Try it now, even with a glass of water: one breath, set it before God, then drink. If you don't pray, let the pause be simple thanks for what's in front of you.

1354.title: Jealous of a conch
1354.hook: Andal questions Vishnu's conch about his lips: why bhakti longs to be near God, and why the conch sounds at worship
1354.carry: bhakti longs to be near god
1354.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava Hindus recite Andal's Nachiyar Tirumoli in temples and homes, and in Vishnu worship the conch is blown and held as one of the Lord's own emblems.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what's offered to god is set apart and the offering a jackal sniffed: her picture of any match but the Lord.
screen: `WHAT'S OFFERED TO GOD IS SET APART.`

segments.voice: Does it smell of camphor? Of the lotus? Is it sweet? A young woman is asking, urgently, and she's asking a seashell. Not any shell: the white conch that rests in the hand of Vishnu, and that Krishna lifts to his lips and blows. She wants to know what his mouth is like, and the conch is the only one who'd know. It's Andal again, in the seventh song of the Nachiyar Tirumoli, and she's jealous of a shell.
screen: `CAMPHOR? THE LOTUS? IS IT SWEET?` → `THE WHITE CONCH.` → `JEALOUS OF A SHELL.`

segments.voice: The opening, in paraphrase: does it smell of camphor, of the lotus, does his coral mouth taste sweet? I long to know. Tell me, white conch of the deep sea, what is the scent and taste of the lips of the one who broke the elephant's tusk? Then the questions turn into complaints. You were born in the ocean, she tells the conch, and now you live in his hand. You rest on his mouth while the rest of us wait. Others can only stand and look at him from afar, and you, a shell, go right up to his lips. It's a love poem, and a funny one: she's envying an object. So why a conch? In the Bhagavad Gita, before the battle, Krishna blows his conch, named Panchajanya. For a Vaishnava listener, the conch isn't decoration. It's one of the Lord's own emblems, held in his hand, carrying his breath. That's why, in many homes and temples, a conch is still blown as worship begins. Now the teaching. Bhakti, loving devotion, isn't content to admire God from far off. It wants to be near. Sri Vaishnava teachers read the conch as a picture of the devotee the Lord keeps closest, so Andal's envy is also a prayer: let me be that close, let my life carry your breath. And the tradition didn't clean her up. It kept a young woman's longing, plain and bodily, taste and scent and jealousy, as a way of talking about God.
screen: `QUESTIONS FOR A SEASHELL` · `THE CONCH IN THE LORD'S HAND` · `WHY THE CONCH SOUNDS AT WORSHIP` · `BHAKTI WANTS TO BE NEAR`

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes a conch is blown at the start of evening worship: one long breath sent through a shell. You don't need one. Breathe in slowly, and on a long breath out, imagine the sound moving through you the way breath moves through the conch. Do it three times. If you pray, let the last breath carry a name of God. If you don't, let it carry a name you love.

1355.title: A thousand elephants
1355.hook: Andal dreams her wedding to the Lord, step by step, and families still sing it to bless their own weddings
1355.carry: the soul's wedding to god blesses ours
1355.howItsDone: Some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's Varanam Ayiram at weddings, and celebrate her marriage to the Lord at her temple in Srivilliputtur and at Srirangam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti longs to be near god: the white conch, camphor or lotus, and a young woman jealous of a shell.

Friend, I had a dream. That's roughly how the song begins, and what follows is a wedding. Elephants first, a thousand of them, the song says, circling round as the groom comes into town. Then the canopy, the drums, the bride's hand taken, the walk around the fire. Every detail is there, the way you'd tell your closest friend the morning after a dream you can't shake. The dreamer is Andal, and the groom is the Lord. Our last day with her: the dream, and the ending tradition gives her.
screen: `FRIEND, I HAD A DREAM.` → `ELEPHANTS, DRUMS, A CANOPY.` → `THE DREAM, AND THE ENDING.`

segments.voice: The song is the sixth in the Nachiyar Tirumoli, named for its opening words, Varanam Ayiram, a thousand elephants. In paraphrase, each verse is one moment of the wedding, and each closes with something like, I dreamed it, friend. The town is decorated. A pavilion goes up, hung with pearls. The groom arrives. The relatives gather; the bride is dressed. He takes her hand. They walk around the sacred fire together. He sets her foot on the grinding stone, one of the steps of the rite. It's a full Tamil wedding, told from the inside, by a bride who hasn't had one. Here's the teaching inside the song. In Sri Vaishnava devotion the Lord is the soul's true beloved, and Andal is the bride every soul is meant to be. So some Sri Vaishnava families sing Varanam Ayiram at their own weddings, and many read it as setting an ordinary marriage inside that bigger one: two people blessed by the soul's wedding to God. Then the ending, as tradition tells it. Her father, Periyalvar, worries: whom can she marry? The story says the Lord of the temple at Srirangam lets it be known that he will take her. So her father brings her there, dressed as a bride. She walks into the shrine, toward the reclining image of the Lord, and isn't seen again. Tradition says she became one with him. The texts are her songs; the ending is the story her community tells. In her poems, the wedding stays a dream.
screen: `A THOUSAND ELEPHANTS` · `THE WEDDING, STEP BY STEP` · `THE LORD AS THE SOUL'S BELOVED` · `THE BRIDE WHO WALKED INTO THE SHRINE`

1356.title: Bells on her ankles
1356.hook: a princess ties bells to her ankles and dances for Krishna, and the town calls her mad: bhakti you can hear
1356.carry: bhakti is love you can hear
1356.howItsDone: Mira's songs are sung as bhajans, with drums and cymbals, in temples, homes and concert halls, and some are danced in classical and folk styles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soul's wedding to god blesses ours: Andal's dream of a wedding, a thousand elephants, and a bride who walked into the shrine. Today, a princess with bells on her feet.
screen: `THE SOUL'S WEDDING TO GOD BLESSES OURS.`

segments.voice: Small brass bells, strung on a cord and tied around the ankles. Every step rings. You can't sneak anywhere wearing them; that's rather the point. Dancers wear them on stage. In one of the songs sung in her name, a princess ties them on and dances, in public, for Krishna. The town talks. Her husband's family is mortified. And the song hides none of it. It repeats what people said about her, and then it shrugs. Year three heard Mira's poison cup and her treasure. Today, her feet.
screen: `BELLS TIED AROUND THE ANKLES.` → `THE TOWN TALKS.` → `TODAY, HER FEET.`

segments.voice: The song opens with the line people know it by, pag ghunghroo bandh Mira nachi re. The sense, in paraphrase: Mira tied bells on her feet and danced. I've made myself my Lord's own servant. People say Mira's gone mad. My mother-in-law says I've ruined the family. And the last line: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and she has met the undying one with ease. First, who's speaking about her. The people, the mother-in-law, the family: the song lets them all have their say. It doesn't argue back. It just goes on dancing. The mother-in-law's word, ruin of the family, shows the line a royal woman crossed by dancing in the open, and the song names it. Second, the word for mad there is bawari, and in Mira's songs madness isn't only an insult. In another song she calls herself prem diwani, mad with love. So the charge the town throws at her becomes something she wears, like the bells. Third, the bells make devotion something you can hear. Bhakti, the way of loving devotion, isn't only a feeling in the chest. In Mira's songs it moves the feet, keeps a rhythm, gathers a crowd. That's why Hindus sing these songs together as bhajans, with a drum and cymbals, in temples and living rooms, and why people sometimes get up and dance. A song about a woman who wouldn't keep still is very hard to sing sitting still.
screen: `MIRA TIED BELLS ON HER FEET` · `THE TOWN HAS ITS SAY` · `MAD, THE WORD SHE WEARS` · `DEVOTION YOU CAN HEAR`

segments.voice: Let one hand tap your knee very softly, in time with the breath, the way cymbals keep time at a bhajan: in, one tap; out, one tap. 1357.title: Only one man in Vrindavan
1357.hook: a holy man in Vrindavan won't meet a woman, and Mira's one sentence teaches how the soul stands before Krishna
1357.carry: before krishna, the soul is the beloved
1357.howItsDone: Vrindavan remains a place of pilgrimage for Krishna devotees, and stories of Mira's time there are told alongside her songs in bhajan gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti is love you can hear with bells on her ankles, dancing while the town called her mad, and wearing the word as her own.

A door, and a message passed through it. On one side, a learned renunciant in Vrindavan who has made a rule for himself: he doesn't meet women. On the other, a woman who has walked a long way to see him, and has just been turned away. She doesn't argue about the rule. She sends back a single sentence, and by the end of the story, the door opens. The woman is Mira, and the sentence is today's whole lesson.
screen: `A DOOR, AND A MESSAGE.` → `A RULE: NO WOMEN.` → `ONE SENTENCE BACK.`

segments.voice: First, where she is. Tradition says that after the troubles with her husband's family, Mira left the palace and took to the road, and came to Vrindavan, the country of Krishna's childhood, where the cowherd girls, the gopis, once ran to the sound of his flute. Holy people and teachers lived there. The story names one of them as Jiva Goswami, a scholar of Krishna devotion; some tellings name another teacher. The story, in paraphrase: Mira asks to meet him. Word comes back that he has vowed not to see women. And Mira answers, roughly: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna. I didn't know anyone else here was claiming to be a man. The renunciant hears it, and comes out to meet her. It's sharp, and it's funny. But under the wit is a teaching that belongs to Vrindavan itself. In the devotion Vrindavan is known for, the soul stands before Krishna the way the gopis did: as the beloved, waiting for him. Before him, no one is the man of the house. That's why poets of this devotion, men included, so often sing in a gopi's voice. So the rule that kept her out rested on a difference that, in that place, she says doesn't count. And she doesn't attack his vow, or his learning, or him. She takes the faith of the place more seriously than the rule does, and lets that speak. Last, this isn't a record anyone wrote down at the door. It's one of the stories told about her, remembered because it teaches, the way a parable does.
screen: `MIRA COMES TO VRINDAVAN` · `A HOLY MAN WHO WON'T MEET WOMEN` · `ONLY ONE MAN IN VRINDAVAN` · `A STORY THAT TEACHES`

segments.voice: Notice the labels you carry today: your job, your role at home, how others see you. Name one quietly, then on an out-breath set it down beside you like a bag. For a few breaths, stand the way the gopis stood before Krishna: no title, only someone who loves and is loved. If you pray, stand before God that way for a moment. If you don't, just be someone breathing.
Mirabai. Turned away in Vrindavan by a holy man who wouldn't meet women, she answered that there was only one man there, Krishna.
Your line: before krishna, the soul is the beloved. Mira said it at a closed door. Rest well.

1358.title: Mira's Lord is Giridhar
1358.hook: Mira's songs end on her own stamp, and every singer at a bhajan steps into a saint's love
1358.carry: a bhajan sings in a saint's footsteps
1358.howItsDone: Mira's songs are sung in bhajan gatherings, temples and concerts, and singers keep her name in the closing line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before Krishna, the soul is the beloved: Mira at a closed door in Vrindavan, answering that there was only one man there.
screen: `BEFORE KRISHNA, THE SOUL IS THE BELOVED.`

segments.voice: This week, three women's voices. Shakuntala, told twice, in an epic and in a play. Andal refusing a mortal groom, questioning a conch, dreaming her wedding. And Mira, dancing in bells and talking her way through a closed door. What reaches us of each one has been carried, retold, sung, by people who loved them. Mira's songs show it plainly, because they end with a signature. To close the week, the last line of a Mira song.
screen: `THREE WOMEN'S VOICES THIS WEEK.` → `CARRIED BY PEOPLE WHO LOVED THEM.` → `THE LAST LINE OF A SONG.`

segments.voice: Listen to how a Mira song ends. Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the clever one who lifted the mountain. The phrase comes back at the close of song after song sung in her name, like a seal pressed into wax. Singers call that kind of closing name a chhap, a stamp. It tells you whose song it is. Now, how do these songs reach us? By being sung: wandering singers, temple gatherings, women singing at home, families passing down the words they knew. And as they're sung, the same song can turn up in different words in different places. So when a song ends with Mira's stamp, what it promises is a voice and a lineage, not a notarized author. That raises an honest question the songs can't settle: which lines go back to Mira's own lips? Some readers sort the songs into older and newer. Others say the question misses the point, since a song stays alive by being sung, changing a little in every mouth. Both views take her seriously. Last, the stamp teaches something about how Hindus pray in song. At a bhajan gathering, a satsang, the company of the good, nobody has to invent their own prayer. You borrow a saint's. Whoever sings Mira's song ends by stepping aside: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord. For a few minutes each singer lends Mira a voice, and Mira lends them her love. That's how a woman who, tradition says, left a palace with almost nothing is still being sung.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR` · `THE CHHAP, A STAMP` · `CARRIED FROM MOUTH TO MOUTH` · `SATSANG: PRAYING IN A SAINT'S WORDS`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one line of a prayer, hymn or song that someone else taught you. Say it or hum it softly, and notice whose words it was before it was yours: the one who made it, and the people who carried it to you, the way singers carried Shakuntala, Andal and Mira this week. Then rest in the breath. If you pray, give thanks for the saints whose words you borrow. If you don't, thank whoever carried them to you.
